title: Mutual authority, seasonal abstinence, and marriage as gift (1 Cor 7)
english: to heal human weakness and to arrange the matters in those places most becomingly; therefore he said a due is owed from the husband and to the husband from the wife. Then, lest he shame those in marriage as being slaves of one another who must not come to the exercise of purity without agreement, he says: The wife does not have authority over her own body, but the husband; likewise also the husband does not have authority over his own body, but the wife. The husband therefore has authority over the wife’s body, and having authority, if he wishes, let him not use the authority; “but we did not use this right,” says the apostle, teaching this, I think, when he says: Do we not have a right to take along a sister as wife, as also the other apostles and the brothers of the Lord and Cephas? (1 Corinthians 9:5). Does the wife then have authority over the husband’s body and is she unable not to use the authority? The word “likewise” set twice gives us to understand that the husband must not think that in the matters of marriage he excels the wife; there is likeness and equality for those married toward one another.

Do not deprive one another, except perhaps by agreement for a time, that you may have leisure for prayer, and be together again (1 Corinthians 7:5). You both ought to know that prayer from a man’s and a woman’s purity is not the same as prayer from intercourse. For if Greeks sometimes practice chastity before idols, how much more you who pray to the God of all? It is good, then, to condescend because of weakness, and to hold back because of prayers. Moses also purifies the people and says for three days not to approach a woman, that by having purified beforehand they may become hearers of God (Exodus 19:15). And in the Kingdoms, when Abathar or Ahimelech the priest wishes to set holy bread before David fleeing Saul’s plot, what does he say except: If the young men are clean from a woman?—not from a strange woman but from a wife (1 Samuel 21:4–5). Then, that someone may receive the bread of the Presence, he ought to be clean from a woman; but that he may receive the greater breads than the Presence, over which the name of God and of Christ and of the Holy Spirit has been invoked, how much more ought someone to be cleaner, that he may truly receive the breads unto salvation and not unto judgment?

Many think “deprive” is said only of gold or silver or something of that sort; but the apostle clearly named deprivation also concerning those in marriages who practice chastity unseasonably and without agreement. Once for all, simply, the one who does not render what is owed deprives the one to whom he owes by not rendering the due. Sometimes a person is shut in so that he cannot render two dues at once; therefore it is written that he may render the necessary due. What I mean will be clear thus: it is not possible both to render prayers to God as one ought and for the married man to render the due to the wife; therefore if the debt toward God presses, one must deprive the other. Hear him saying: Do not deprive one another, except perhaps by agreement for a time, that you may have leisure for prayer and be together again—as if prayer sent up is not pure even for those who have come together, even if they have come together lawfully. One must also abstain from a woman in the time of her period, and it is counted a great charge to come together with a woman who is in her period. In Ezekiel’s catalog of brave deeds and of sins it is written that he will not approach a woman in her separation (Ezekiel 18:6). And one must be wholly pure also from one’s own wife in a time of prayer and fasting.

And again, he says, be together, lest Satan tempt you because of your lack of self-control. This I say by way of concession, not of command (1 Corinthians 7:5–6). Everywhere he loosens the word because of weakness, and again tightens it to turn the hearers. I wish all people to be as I myself am. But each has his own gift from God, one in this way and another in that (1 Corinthians 7:7). Marriage breathes of gift when the measures are kept—those of agreement. And one can truly say of some that for this one marriage is a gift, when there is no disorder, when there is all peace, all agreement. Yet to say that marriage of a believer with a Gentile woman, or of a Gentile with a believing woman, is a gift from God—this I would not say. For the gift of God cannot reach the Gentiles; if she believes, if she is saved, then she will begin to receive the gift.

title: Against Marcion; widows, remarriage, and unequally yoked (1 Cor 7)
english: Those from Marcion also use this saying, and without sense they forbid marriage, saying that chastity is a command of the other god whom they invented beside the Creator. Yet from the saying itself one can prove to them that they forbid marriage badly, and badly divide the Godhead. For if there is a gift to one in this way and to another in that, marriage also is a gift; if marriage is a gift, marriage the gift is badly forbidden; if the one in this way and the other in that are from God, it is clear that one God is the giver of chastity and the giver of marriage, and one is the God of the law and of the gospel, whom the prophets first proclaimed and later Christ Jesus.

But I say to the unmarried and to the widows that it is good for them if they remain as I also am; but if they are not practicing self-control, let them marry, for it is better to marry than to burn. To the married I give charge—not I but the Lord—that a wife not be separated from a husband—but if she is separated, let her remain unmarried or be reconciled to the husband—and that a husband not send away a wife. To the rest I say, I not the Lord (1 Corinthians 7:8–12).

Some among us teach beyond what is written; and thinking they are doing something, when they ought to exhort to single marriage without laying a snare on those who cannot, they do not do this, but impose necessity and wish not to gather the twice-married nor to share with them as with those who have transgressed, not respecting even the apostle’s voices. For the one who says to the unmarried and the widows, if they are not continent let them marry, openly permitted after the first marriage, after a woman has been widowed, to marry—while blaming the one who marries and the one who is married; for he said: If they are not continent, let them marry. See whether not being continent is not already an accusation—as when it is said to Christian people: Better to marry than to burn—he naming as burning the desire of the flesh not quenched by the Word but mastering the sinner’s soul. We therefore, taught by the apostle, do not forbid remarriage; for by comparison with burning, remarriage is more choiceworthy. Yet when something is thought better by comparison with evils, that thing is clearly not good. The second marriage is not temperance; it is not according to the nature of Adam the first-formed; for one cannot say to the second wife: This now is bone of my bones and flesh of my flesh (Genesis 2:23). Abraham had also Hagar, and came to be also with Keturah; yet when he died, none was laid with him except the wife by nature; for Abraham and Sarah were in the tomb. And Jacob too, even if he had been with Rachel and with Leah and also with the maidservants, yet in the tomb only Leah was with him. With the mystical economy of the fathers; yet surely even now the one who takes a second does not say: I am fulfilling a mystical economy. For Paul will come saying: Tell me, you who read the law, do you not hear the law? For it is written: So-and-so had two sons, and so on; it will not also be said over him: These things are allegorized, for these women are two covenants; for these things happened typically to them, but were written for us upon whom the ends of the ages have come (Galatians 4:21–24; 1 Corinthians 10:11).

I say to the widows and to the unmarried that it is good for them if they remain as I also am. This is a second good; for there is another good first before this: it is good for a man not to touch a woman. What second good? It is good for them if they remain as I also am; but if they are not continent, let them marry; for it is better to marry than to burn. Therefore those in first marriages who have not yet experienced second ones should practice chastity, that if something human happens they may not, caught untrained, behave shamefully. Better, then, to marry a second marriage—for he does not mean the first here, as is clear from the wording “to burn.” From here he passes to another legislation: To the married I give charge, not I but the Lord; the legislation toward the married is not from me but from the Lord. At the same time he keeps a necessary observation: he named “married” when both are believers, both the husband and the wife. That he did not name among the married the others who are unequally yoked is clear from his adding: To the rest I say, I not the Lord. Are the rest then not married? He does not measure them as married; for on these a wife is not fitted to a husband from God; but on the believers, when both share and

title: Lord’s charge, holiness in mixed marriage, circumcision paradigm (1 Cor 7)
english: of prayers and of holy childbearing and of all things in which Christians must share, he says that marriage is not alien to God. I charge, then—not I but the Lord—that a wife not be separated from a husband. The primary point is this: a yoking that has already been bound must not be loosed. But if she is also separated—for many causes of separation can arise; for example if fornication happens to the wife, it is a sin to keep the wife who has fornicated. If then she is also separated and some cause of separation arises, let her remain unmarried or be reconciled to the husband. Likewise I also want a husband to be such that he not send away a wife. To the rest I say, I not the Lord. To those who have married I do not legislate, but the Lord; to those not married but unequally yoked with unbelievers I do not have a law to give from God; for they are not even worthy of God’s laws; but let them hear us. And I will use what is written in the law to make the matters of the place understood. The laws according to Moses—some are God’s, and some are Moses’. And knowing this difference of God’s laws and Moses’ laws, the Lord said concerning those legislated by God: For God said, Honor father and mother; and concerning those by Moses: Moses, because of your hardness of heart, allowed you to dismiss your wives (Matthew 19:8). If you keep the matters of the book of divorce you will find the law written not from a command of the Lord. Moses then, serving God, gave second laws beside the laws of God; Paul, serving the gospel, gave second laws to those of the church after the laws from God through Jesus Christ. And it is good to hear laws from the Lord rather than to hear laws of Paul the apostle. For even if he is holy, still he has laws far lesser than the laws of the Lord.

For the unbelieving husband is made holy in the wife, and the unbelieving wife is made holy in the brother (1 Corinthians 7:14). As a kind of blending happens of the two, husband and wife, into one flesh, as of wine and water; and as the believer imparts holiness to the Gentile spouse, or the reverse—the believing woman to the unbelieving husband—so also the unbeliever imparts pollution to the believing wife, or the unbelieving wife to the believing husband. Why then does he say the unbeliever is made holy by receiving something from the believer, and is not also profaned by receiving something from the unbelieving part? For each, conversing from the abundance of the heart with the other, either imparts or receives, and in time the one entirely conquers the other. And what need, he says, of such a contest and danger? For either he will succeed or fail, and either he will lose his soul as well or, after much toil, scarcely be able to gain. Therefore it is good, before a person is forestalled, carefully to look not only at this but also at what is coming, and having looked either not to marry or, marrying, to marry in the Lord. For a wife is bound as long as her husband lives; but if the husband dies, she is free to be married to whom she wishes, only in the Lord (1 Corinthians 7:39). We do not hear the “only in the Lord,” but we read “she is free to be married to whom she wishes,” and we no longer set beside it “only in the Lord.” And yet even there, when he said “only in the Lord,” he again checked the word saying she is more blessed if she remains so, according to my judgment. So the apostle, having said the more auspicious thing—“For she is made holy”—left us to understand the other.

Was anyone called circumcised? Let him not become uncircumcised. Was anyone called in uncircumcision? Let him not be circumcised. Circumcision is nothing and uncircumcision is nothing, but keeping God’s commandments. Let each remain in the calling in which he was called (1 Corinthians 7:18–20). It will seem that he has unseasonably cast beside the word about marriage and chastity, since no inquiry had arisen about those from circumcision who believe not needing to draw the foreskin, and again those in uncircumcision not needing to be circumcised, and about “Were you called a slave? Do not be concerned,” and what follows. Perhaps then he took slavery and freedom as a paradigm of the married and the unmarried, calling circumcised the one who has put away the wife and uncircumcised the one who has married?
